texts.title: The profile I chose not to delete
paragraphs: When I was fifteen, I created a second social-media account that none of my relatives knew about. On my public account I posted family celebrations, school events and carefully chosen travel photos. On the smaller account I shared unfinished drawings, awkward jokes and opinions I was still testing. At first I thought one account showed the real me and the other was a performance. Later I realized that both were selective.

The difference became obvious when I considered deleting the smaller account before applying for a summer programme. I worried that an old joke might be misunderstood by someone who did not know the context. Yet deleting everything also felt dishonest. Those posts showed interests and friendships that mattered to me, even if they did not fit the tidy version of myself presented elsewhere.

A media-literacy teacher helped me rethink the problem. She said identity online is not a simple choice between truth and deception. Every profile involves decisions about audience, privacy and purpose. The useful question is not whether a profile is perfectly complete, because no profile can be, but whether the choices we make create a seriously misleading impression.

I kept the account but changed its privacy settings and removed two posts that included other people who had not agreed to be visible. The experience made me more cautious, but not more secretive. I now see digital identity as editing rather than inventing: the challenge is to decide what belongs in each context without pretending that one edited version contains the whole person.

questions.prompt: What assumption did the writer initially make about the two accounts?
options: Both accounts were completely false.
One was the real self and the other was a performance.
Relatives preferred the smaller account.
The public account contained unfinished work.
questions.explanationJa: 最初は一方がreal self、もう一方がperformanceだと考えていました。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons the writer hesitated to delete the smaller account.
markscheme: Deleting it could erase evidence of interests or friendships that mattered to the writer.
The posts were part of the writer's genuine experience even if they did not match the tidy public image.
questions.explanationJa: 不完全な投稿でも、自分の関心や人間関係の一部だったためです。

questions.prompt: True or false: The teacher believed a good profile should show a person's complete identity.
questions.justification: She says no profile can be perfectly complete and that profiles are shaped by audience, privacy and purpose.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。完全なprofileは不可能だと述べています。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'giving a wrong idea about something'.
questions.explanationJa: misleading＝誤解を招く、誤った印象を与える。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, what does 'Those posts' refer to?
options: Posts on the smaller account
Programme application forms
Travel photos on the public account
Messages from relatives
questions.explanationJa: smaller accountにあるunfinished drawingsやjokesなどを指します。

questions.prompt: What two practical changes did the writer make after reconsidering the account?
markscheme: The writer changed the account's privacy settings.
The writer removed posts showing people who had not agreed to be visible.
questions.explanationJa: privacy設定の変更と、他人の同意のない投稿削除です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: The writer now sees digital identity as ________ rather than inventing.
questions.explanationJa: 本文は editing rather than inventing です。

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude at the end?
options: All online profiles are deceptive.
Digital identity requires contextual choices rather than one complete version of the self.
People should delete all old posts.
Private accounts should never exist.
questions.explanationJa: contextごとに何を見せるかを選ぶ必要があるという立場です。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the essay? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: To reflect on how online identity is selectively presented rather than completely shown.
To argue that responsible editing should consider audience, privacy and the rights of other people.
questions.explanationJa: online identityのselective natureとresponsible editingが主題です。

texts.title: The year I learned to ask for directions
paragraphs: During my exchange year in Montreal, I became strangely proud of never asking for directions. I could use maps on my phone, translate signs and calculate routes without speaking to anyone. I told myself this proved I was independent. In reality, I was often so focused on avoiding mistakes that I experienced the city as a sequence of instructions rather than a place full of people.

One rainy evening my phone battery died while I was trying to find a community theatre. After walking in circles for twenty minutes, I finally asked a woman at a bus stop for help. She did not simply point toward the theatre. She explained that the road ahead was closed, suggested a different bus and asked why I was going there. By the time the bus arrived, we had discussed local theatre, winter weather and the neighbourhood where she had grown up.

That conversation changed how I thought about independence. Depending on others for small pieces of information did not make me less capable. In fact, asking a clear question often required more confidence than silently following an app. It also created opportunities that efficient technology had removed from my routine.

I still use digital maps, especially when I am late or travelling somewhere unsafe. The lesson was not to reject technology but to notice what it changes. A tool can solve the problem of getting lost while also reducing the chance of an unexpected conversation. Good travel, I learned, sometimes means choosing the slower solution when speed is not the only thing that matters.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer avoid asking for directions at first?
options: The writer could not speak the local language.
The writer associated solving routes alone with independence.
People in Montreal refused to help visitors.
The writer disliked using a phone.
questions.explanationJa: 一人でrouteを解決することをindependenceの証明だと考えていました。

questions.prompt: Give two ways the woman at the bus stop helped the writer.
markscheme: She explained that the road ahead was closed.
She suggested a different bus and/or gave alternative route information.
questions.explanationJa: 単なる方向指示ではなく、road closureとalternative busを教えました。

questions.prompt: True or false: The writer concludes that asking for help is a sign of weak independence.
questions.justification: The writer says asking a clear question can require confidence and does not make a person less capable.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。helpを求めることにもconfidenceが必要だと考え直しています。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'able to do things successfully'.
questions.explanationJa: capable＝能力がある。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, what does 'what it changes' refer to?
options: The effects technology has on the experience of travelling
The weather in Montreal
The theatre programme
The writer's exchange-school timetable
questions.explanationJa: technologyがtravel experienceをどう変えるかを指します。

questions.prompt: Give two benefits the writer now associates with asking people for help.
markscheme: It can build or require confidence rather than reduce independence.
It can create unexpected conversations or social connections.
questions.explanationJa: confidenceとunexpected conversationの2点です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 1: The writer experienced the city as a sequence of ________.
questions.explanationJa: 本文は a sequence of instructions です。

questions.prompt: What is the writer's final view of technology?
options: Digital maps should never be used.
Technology is useful, but efficiency can remove valuable human encounters.
Only tourists should ask for directions.
Getting lost is always better than arriving quickly.
questions.explanationJa: technologyを否定せず、efficiencyのtrade-offを意識しています。

questions.prompt: Why is the title appropriate? Give two ideas.
markscheme: The writer literally learned to ask other people for directions.
The experience represents a broader change in the writer's understanding of independence and human connection.
questions.explanationJa: literalな経験とindependence観の変化の両方を表すtitleです。

texts.title: A robot in the care home?
paragraphs: A care home in Leeds has begun testing small mobile robots that can carry laundry, deliver water and remind residents about scheduled activities. The machines are not designed to provide medical treatment or replace care workers. Managers say the goal is to remove repetitive tasks so staff can spend more time in direct conversation with residents.

Early reactions have been mixed. Some residents enjoy naming the robots and treating them as part of the daily routine. Others find the machines distracting or dislike being reminded about activities by a synthetic voice. Staff have also discovered practical limitations: narrow corridors can confuse the sensors, and a robot cannot easily judge whether a resident is tired, upset or simply wants to be left alone.

Ethicist Dr Nina Cole argues that the important question is not whether a task can be automated, but what kind of relationship the task contains. Carrying towels may involve little emotional meaning, while helping someone eat can include dignity, trust and subtle communication. Cole warns that efficiency becomes dangerous when managers measure only the time saved and ignore the human value hidden inside apparently simple tasks.

The care home has therefore created a rule: robots may assist with logistics, but decisions involving personal care remain with staff. The trial will also measure resident satisfaction, staff workload and the number of meaningful conversations, not only cost. Managers say the technology will be considered successful only if it increases human attention rather than merely reducing labour.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason the care home is testing robots?
options: To replace all care workers
To reduce repetitive tasks and free staff for direct interaction
To provide medical diagnosis
To entertain visitors
questions.explanationJa: repetitive tasksを減らしてstaffのdirect conversation時間を増やす目的です。

questions.prompt: Give two limitations of the robots mentioned in paragraph 2.
markscheme: Narrow corridors can confuse their sensors.
They cannot easily judge emotional states or whether a resident wants privacy.
questions.explanationJa: sensorの物理的限界とemotion判断の限界です。

questions.prompt: True or false: Dr Cole believes all simple-looking tasks have little human meaning.
questions.justification: She says apparently simple tasks can contain dignity, trust or subtle communication, depending on the relationship involved.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。simpleに見えるtaskにもhuman valueがある場合があります。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'respect for a person's worth'.
questions.explanationJa: dignity＝尊厳。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'the human value' refer to?
options: The emotional and relational importance within some care tasks
The purchase price of the robots
The physical size of the care home
The speed of laundry delivery
questions.explanationJa: care taskに含まれるdignityやtrustなどを指します。

questions.prompt: What two principles are built into the care home's rule for robot use?
markscheme: Robots may help with logistics or repetitive practical tasks.
Personal-care decisions remain with human staff.
questions.explanationJa: logisticsはrobot、personal careはhuman staffという境界です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Success requires technology to increase human ________.
questions.explanationJa: increase human attention がkey phraseです。

questions.prompt: What is Dr Cole's attitude toward automation?
options: Completely opposed to all automation
Supportive only when efficiency is considered together with human relationships
Certain robots can replace emotional care
Interested only in reducing costs
questions.explanationJa: automationそのものではなく、relationshipの価値を見落とさない条件付きの立場です。

questions.prompt: Why will the trial measure more than cost? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Managers want to know whether residents are satisfied and/or staff workload improves.
They want evidence that meaningful human interaction increases rather than merely labour costs falling.
questions.explanationJa: cost以外にresident satisfaction、workload、meaningful conversationsを評価します。

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose?
options: To advertise a particular robot company
To present benefits and limits of automation in a human-care setting
To prove care homes should ban technology
To explain how robot sensors are manufactured
questions.explanationJa: care settingでのautomationのbenefitとlimitをbalancedに示すreportです。

texts.title: The bus pass experiment
paragraphs: The city of Harbridge has launched a six-month trial offering free bus travel to residents aged sixteen to eighteen. The council hopes the pass will help students reach school, part-time work and social activities without depending on parents or expensive taxi journeys.

Supporters argue that the policy is also a test of long-term travel habits. If teenagers become comfortable using public transport before they learn to drive, they may be less likely to rely on private cars later. Critics reply that the trial is too narrow because young people living in outer districts still face buses that run only once an hour.

Transport officials accept that price is only one barrier. They have added two evening services on the busiest routes and are collecting data about missed connections, journey times and crowding. However, expanding every route immediately would be expensive, so the council says the trial must reveal where additional services have the greatest effect.

Student groups welcome the free pass but want the council to judge success carefully. A rise in passenger numbers is useful evidence, they say, but it does not show whether students can actually reach evening jobs or return home safely. The council has promised to publish both ridership figures and survey results before deciding whether the scheme should continue.

questions.prompt: What is one immediate purpose of the free bus pass?
options: To replace all school buses
To help teenagers travel independently to school, work and activities
To increase taxi use
To encourage students to buy cars
questions.explanationJa: school・work・activitiesへのindependent travel支援です。

questions.prompt: Give two arguments supporters make for the policy.
markscheme: It reduces transport cost or dependence on parents/taxis for teenagers.
It may build public-transport habits before young people begin driving.
questions.explanationJa: immediate accessとlong-term habit formationの2点です。

questions.prompt: True or false: Officials believe making buses free solves every transport barrier.
questions.justification: Officials say price is only one barrier and are also examining service frequency, missed connections and journey times.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。service frequencyなど非価格要因もあります。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'the number of people using a transport service'.
questions.explanationJa: ridership＝交通機関の利用者数。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, what does 'the trial' refer to?
options: The six-month free bus-pass scheme
A driving test
A taxi subsidy
A school timetable
questions.explanationJa: free bus travel schemeを指します。

questions.prompt: What two kinds of evidence will officials use to decide where extra services are needed?
markscheme: Operational data such as missed connections, journey times or crowding.
Passenger or student feedback gathered through surveys.
questions.explanationJa: operational dataとuser surveyの両方です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 3: Expanding every route immediately would be ________.
questions.explanationJa: 本文の直接表現です。

questions.prompt: What concern do student groups raise about measuring success?
options: Passenger numbers alone may not show whether useful journeys are actually possible.
Surveys should never be used.
Only taxi journeys should be counted.
The scheme should end before data is collected.
questions.explanationJa: ridershipだけではreal accessを十分測れないという指摘です。

questions.prompt: What is the main tension presented in the report? Give two sides.
markscheme: Free fares can improve access and encourage public-transport habits.
Service frequency and route quality may still limit the policy, especially in outer areas.
questions.explanationJa: price supportのbenefitとservice limitationのtrade-offです。

texts.title: Why family recipes change
paragraphs: When chef Mina Park published her grandmother's dumpling recipe online, several readers complained that one ingredient was 'not traditional'. Park had used locally available mushrooms instead of the variety her grandmother bought in Korea. The criticism surprised her because the family recipe had already changed many times before reaching her kitchen.

Her grandmother had adapted the filling after moving abroad, replacing expensive ingredients and adjusting the seasoning to what her children would eat. Park's mother later reduced the salt for health reasons. Each generation described the dish as the same family recipe even though no version was identical.

Food historian Leah Morgan says this is common. Traditions survive partly because people repeat them, but also because they adapt them. A recipe that cannot respond to migration, cost, climate or changing tastes may disappear rather than remain perfectly preserved. For Morgan, authenticity is better understood as a relationship with history than as an exact list of ingredients.

Park now includes a note beside the recipe explaining the changes made by each generation. She says this does not weaken the family's connection to the dish. Instead, the changes show how the family carried the recipe through different places and circumstances. The recipe is traditional, she argues, precisely because people cared enough to keep making it.

questions.prompt: Why did some readers criticize Park's recipe?
options: She refused to publish it.
She used a different type of mushroom.
She removed all seasoning.
She claimed to invent dumplings.
questions.explanationJa: traditionalでないmushroomを使ったと批判されました。

questions.prompt: Give two examples of how earlier generations changed the recipe.
markscheme: The grandmother replaced expensive ingredients or adjusted seasoning after migration.
Park's mother reduced the salt for health reasons.
questions.explanationJa: migration・cost・taste・healthに応じた変更です。

questions.prompt: True or false: Morgan believes tradition survives only when nothing changes.
questions.justification: Morgan says traditions survive through both repetition and adaptation, and a recipe unable to adapt may disappear.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。adaptationもtradition survivalの一部です。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'the quality of being genuine or true to its origin'.
questions.explanationJa: authenticity＝真正性。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, what does 'the changes' refer to?
options: The adaptations made to the recipe by different generations
Changes to the website design
Readers' complaints
Restaurant prices
questions.explanationJa: generationごとのrecipe adaptationsを指します。

questions.prompt: According to Morgan, why can adaptation help a tradition survive? Give two factors.
markscheme: Adaptation allows a practice to respond to conditions such as migration, cost or climate.
It allows the tradition to fit changing tastes or circumstances instead of disappearing.
questions.explanationJa: 環境や生活条件に合わせられることでcontinuityが生まれます。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 3: Authenticity is a relationship with ________.
questions.explanationJa: relationship with history が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is Park's attitude toward the recipe changes?
options: She sees them as evidence that the tradition has failed.
She sees them as part of how the family preserved the tradition.
She wants to return to one exact original version.
She believes family recipes should never be published.
questions.explanationJa: changesそのものがtraditionをcarryした証拠だと見ています。

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the feature? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: Tradition does not necessarily require exact sameness across generations.
Adaptation can express continuity, care and connection to history.
questions.explanationJa: traditionとchangeを対立させないことが主題です。

texts.title: Volunteering after the flood
paragraphs: After severe flooding damaged homes in her town, sixteen-year-old Elena Ruiz joined a weekend volunteer team. She expected to spend most of her time carrying boxes and cleaning floors. Instead, the task she remembers most involved sitting in a temporary shelter and listening to an older resident describe the objects she had lost.

At first Elena felt useless because she could not replace the photographs, letters or furniture being discussed. A coordinator explained that disaster support is not always about solving a problem immediately. People may need practical help, accurate information or simply time to explain what happened without being rushed.

The team received training on boundaries as well as kindness. Volunteers were told not to promise financial support, give medical advice or post photographs of residents without permission. They also learned to pass serious concerns to trained staff. Elena says these rules initially felt formal, but she later understood that good intentions do not automatically make every action helpful.

The experience changed her idea of volunteering. She still values visible tasks such as distributing supplies, but she no longer measures usefulness by how dramatic a result looks. Sometimes the most responsible action is to listen, give correct information or recognize that someone else has the expertise required.

questions.prompt: What surprised Elena about her volunteering experience?
options: She did no practical work at all.
A memorable and useful task involved listening rather than fixing something.
Residents refused all support.
The flood caused no property damage.
questions.explanationJa: problem-solvingではなくlisteningが重要なtaskになったことが意外でした。

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, give two different forms of support people may need after a disaster.
markscheme: Practical help and/or accurate information.
Time to talk about what happened or be listened to without being rushed.
questions.explanationJa: practical support、information、listeningから2点です。

questions.prompt: True or false: Volunteers were encouraged to use good intentions as their only guide.
questions.justification: They were trained in boundaries and told not to make promises, give medical advice or share photographs without permission.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。good intentionsだけでは不十分でboundariesが必要です。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'limits on what a person should do'.
questions.explanationJa: boundaries＝行動範囲・限界。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'these rules' refer to?
options: The limits and safeguarding instructions given to volunteers
The flood-warning system
The residents' house rules
The town's parking rules
questions.explanationJa: promise、medical advice、photo permissionなどのrulesです。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons the rules can make volunteering more responsible.
markscheme: They prevent volunteers from giving advice or promises beyond their competence.
They protect residents' privacy and ensure serious concerns reach trained staff.
questions.explanationJa: competenceとprivacy/safeguardingを守ります。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Elena no longer measures usefulness by how ________ a result looks.
questions.explanationJa: dramatic が本文のkeywordです。

questions.prompt: What is Elena's attitude toward visible practical tasks at the end?
options: She thinks they are useless.
She still values them but no longer sees them as the only form of useful help.
She believes only trained staff should distribute supplies.
She refuses to do them again.
questions.explanationJa: visible taskも評価しつつ、それだけをusefulnessの基準にしません。

questions.prompt: How did Elena's definition of useful help change? Give two ideas.
markscheme: She moved from valuing mainly visible problem-solving to recognizing listening and accurate information as useful.
She learned that responsible help can include recognizing limits and referring problems to people with appropriate expertise.
questions.explanationJa: useful helpをbroaderかつresponsibleに捉えるようになりました。

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose?
options: To present volunteering as easy work
To show how disaster volunteering can teach both empathy and limits
To criticize trained coordinators
To argue that teenagers should provide medical advice
questions.explanationJa: empathyだけでなくboundariesも学ぶexperienceとして描いています。

texts.title: When the museum went digital
paragraphs: When the Westbridge Museum digitized thousands of objects from its collection, staff expected the website mainly to attract people who could not visit in person. Instead, local visitors began using the online archive before coming to the building, searching for particular objects and planning what they wanted to see.

Curators soon noticed a second effect. High-resolution images allowed viewers to zoom in on details that were difficult to see through display cases. However, digital access also removed scale, texture and the physical sense of standing beside an object. A tiny jewellery box and a two-metre sculpture could appear almost equal on a phone screen.

The museum responded by adding measurements, short videos and photographs showing objects beside familiar items. It also created themed online collections that connect objects currently displayed in different rooms. Curator Malik Ahmed says the goal is not to reproduce the physical museum perfectly. Digital media should do what it does well while making its limits visible.

The project has therefore changed the museum's definition of access. Access no longer means simply opening the building's doors or putting photographs online. It means helping different audiences understand what they can and cannot learn from each format, and allowing online and physical visits to support one another.

questions.prompt: What unexpected use did local visitors make of the online archive?
options: They used it to prepare for physical visits.
They stopped visiting the museum completely.
They bought the digitized objects.
They used it only for school exams.
questions.explanationJa: physical visitのplanningにonline archiveを使いました。

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one limitation of high-resolution digital images.
markscheme: Advantage: viewers can zoom in on small details that may be hard to see in display cases.
Limitation: digital images can hide physical scale, texture or the experience of being beside the object.
questions.explanationJa: detail accessとphysical context lossのcontrastです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Ahmed wants the digital museum to copy the physical museum exactly.
questions.justification: He says digital media should do what it does well while making its limits visible rather than reproducing the physical museum perfectly.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。digital独自のstrengthとlimitを明示する方針です。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'the size of something when measured'.
questions.explanationJa: measurements＝寸法・測定値。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, what does 'each format' refer to?
options: Online and physical ways of experiencing the collection
Different ticket prices
Different school subjects
Different languages
questions.explanationJa: online formatとphysical formatです。

questions.prompt: Give two ways the museum tried to make digital objects easier to understand.
markscheme: It added measurements, videos or photographs showing scale through familiar objects.
It created themed online collections connecting objects across different physical rooms.
questions.explanationJa: scale/context情報とthemed connectionsです。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 3: Digital media should make its ________ visible.
questions.explanationJa: make its limits visible が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is the article's main attitude toward digitization?
options: Entirely negative
Positive but attentive to what digital access cannot reproduce
Certain physical museums are unnecessary
Focused only on website design
questions.explanationJa: benefitを認めつつlimitationsも明確にしています。

questions.prompt: How has the museum's idea of access changed? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Access now means more than simply entering the building or seeing images online.
It includes helping audiences understand the strengths and limits of each format and making online and physical experiences support each other.
questions.explanationJa: accessを単なるavailabilityからmeaningful understandingへ広げています。

texts.title: Who gets to use the school gym?
paragraphs: A secondary school in Westmere has opened its sports hall to local community groups on weekday evenings. The decision followed a council report showing that nearby neighbourhoods had few affordable indoor exercise spaces. The school receives a small maintenance payment, while registered groups can book the hall at below-commercial rates.

The first term was popular, but conflicts quickly appeared. Basketball clubs wanted long evening sessions, older residents preferred early times and school teams sometimes needed the hall unexpectedly before competitions. A simple first-come, first-served booking system gave an advantage to groups with volunteers able to log in as soon as bookings opened.

The school replaced that system with a monthly allocation process. Groups now state the number of participants, the age range they serve and whether they have access to other facilities. No single factor guarantees a booking, but the information helps staff compare need rather than only speed. Some clubs dislike the extra paperwork, while others say the new system is fairer.

The principal says fairness does not mean every group receives the same number of hours. A small disability-sport programme may need a particular accessible time slot even if a larger club could fill the hall more often. The school will review the rules after six months using attendance data, cancellations and feedback from both students and community users.

questions.prompt: Why did the school open the sports hall to community groups?
options: The school stopped using it.
Nearby areas had limited affordable indoor exercise space.
Commercial gyms requested it.
The council banned school sport.
questions.explanationJa: communityにaffordable indoor spaceが不足していたためです。

questions.prompt: Give two problems with the original first-come, first-served system.
markscheme: Different groups needed conflicting time slots for different reasons.
Groups with volunteers available at booking time had an unfair speed advantage.
questions.explanationJa: time conflictとdigital/availability advantageです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Under the new system, the largest group automatically receives priority.
questions.justification: No single factor guarantees a booking; staff compare several indicators of need and access to alternatives.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。participant numberだけでは決まりません。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'the process of distributing something for particular uses'.
questions.explanationJa: allocation＝配分。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'the information' refer to?
options: Participant numbers, age range and access to other facilities
Commercial gym prices
School exam results
Volunteer names only
questions.explanationJa: new allocationで提出するneed-related informationです。

questions.prompt: Why might a small disability-sport programme receive a valuable time slot? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: It may have specific accessibility requirements or fewer suitable alternative times/facilities.
The system defines fairness by need rather than giving identical hours or simply rewarding the largest group.
questions.explanationJa: equal hoursではなくneed-based fairnessを示すexampleです。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Fairness does not mean every group receives the same number of ________.
questions.explanationJa: same number of hours が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is the principal's view of fairness?
options: Fairness always means identical treatment.
Fairness may require different treatment when needs differ.
Only school teams should receive priority.
Fairness cannot be measured at all.
questions.explanationJa: different needsに応じたdifferent treatmentもfairと考えています。

questions.prompt: Why will the school review several types of evidence after six months?
markscheme: Attendance and cancellation data can show how effectively bookings are actually used.
Feedback from students and community users can show whether the rules feel workable and fair to different groups.
questions.explanationJa: usage dataとstakeholder feedbackを組み合わせてevaluationします。

texts.title: The beach after the tourists leave
paragraphs: Every autumn, volunteers on the island of San Riva collect rubbish from beaches after the tourist season. Plastic bottles are easy to identify, but a growing share of the waste comes from items designed to be used only briefly: broken beach toys, cheap umbrellas and disposable picnic equipment. Local environmental groups say the problem is not simply littering but a tourism economy built around convenience.

The council first responded by adding more bins, yet surveys showed that bins alone had limited effect. Some products were too large to fit, while visitors often left unwanted equipment beside bins believing someone else might reuse it. In practice, many of these objects became waste after rain or wind damaged them.

A new programme asks rental shops and hotels to collect reusable beach equipment at the end of a visitor's stay. Participating businesses receive a small reduction in waste fees if they repair, rent again or donate a minimum percentage of returned items. The council is also working with shops to stock fewer extremely cheap products that are difficult to repair.

Not everyone supports the policy. Some retailers fear that higher-quality products will cost more and discourage budget travellers. Environmental groups reply that low prices can hide costs paid later through cleanup, landfill and pollution. The council will review sales, visitor surveys, waste volume and repair rates before deciding whether the programme should expand.

questions.prompt: What broader problem do environmental groups identify in paragraph 1?
options: Tourists never use beaches.
The tourism economy encourages short-lived convenience products.
All beach waste comes from local residents.
Plastic bottles are impossible to recycle.
questions.explanationJa: individual litteringだけでなくshort-lived convenience modelを問題視しています。

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why adding more bins did not solve the problem.
markscheme: Some unwanted items were too large to fit into bins.
Visitors left items beside bins for possible reuse, but weather often damaged them and turned them into waste.
questions.explanationJa: sizeとfalse expectation of reuseが原因です。

questions.prompt: True or false: Businesses receive the waste-fee reduction simply for collecting returned items.
questions.justification: They must repair, rent again or donate a minimum percentage of returned items to receive the reduction.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。collectionだけでなくreuse outcomeが必要です。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'a place where waste is buried'.
questions.explanationJa: landfill＝埋立地。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'Participating businesses' refer to?
options: Rental shops and hotels joining the collection programme
All tourists on the island
Only environmental charities
Beach-cleaning volunteers
questions.explanationJa: programme参加のrental shops/hotelsです。

questions.prompt: Give two ways the new programme tries to reduce waste before disposal.
markscheme: It creates a return system so equipment can be repaired, rented again or donated.
It encourages shops to stock fewer very cheap products that are difficult to repair.
questions.explanationJa: reuse systemとproduct selectionの両方です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Retailers worry higher-quality products may discourage ________ travellers.
questions.explanationJa: budget travellers が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is the environmental groups' response to the price concern?
options: Low prices may hide environmental and cleanup costs paid later.
All tourists should receive free equipment.
Cleanup has no cost.
Higher prices always reduce tourism.
questions.explanationJa: cheap priceがexternal costsを隠しているというargumentです。

questions.prompt: Why will the council examine both sales and waste data? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Sales and visitor surveys can show whether the policy affects affordability or tourist behaviour.
Waste volume and repair rates can show whether the programme actually reduces disposal and increases reuse.
questions.explanationJa: economic/social impactとenvironmental outcomeの両方を評価します。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the article?
options: To argue that tourism should end
To examine a policy that shifts beach-waste prevention toward reuse and producer participation
To advertise cheap beach toys
To explain how to build more bins
questions.explanationJa: reuseとbusiness responsibilityを軸にしたpolicy evaluationです。
